# Ammonia Smell from Exhaust: Diagnosing an Infinity G35 After Pipe Replacement

A distinct ammonia odor drifting into the cabin while driving is a classic chemical signature of unburned urea slipping past the emission control system. In the context of your Infinity G35, which likely utilizes a Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system to meet modern emission standards, this smell is rarely cosmetic; it is a diagnostic flag indicating that nitrogen oxides ($NO_x$) are not being neutralized correctly. Since you recently replaced the exhaust pipe, the root cause could range from a simple installation oversight to a deeper failure in the SCR architecture itself.

The core mechanism relies on Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF), also known as urea solution. This fluid is injected into the exhaust stream upstream of the catalytic converter. When heated, the urea decomposes into ammonia ($NH_3$) and carbon dioxide. The catalyst then facilitates a reaction where this ammonia reduces $NO_x$ into harmless nitrogen gas and water. If you smell ammonia, it means the reduction efficiency has dropped below a critical threshold, or the ammonia is bypassing the catalyst entirely before reacting.

Given your recent exhaust pipe replacement, the first suspect is physical blockage or improper routing. An exhaust system is designed to maintain specific backpressure levels and gas velocities. If the new pipe was installed with an internal obstruction, bent into a restrictive angle, or if heat shields were omitted leading to premature catalytic converter overheating, the flow dynamics change. This can cause the urea droplets to condense on cooler surfaces within the new piping rather than staying in the gas phase where the reaction occurs. Condensed urea sitting in a dip or low point of a new pipe can also evaporate later as hot exhaust gases pass through, releasing raw ammonia directly into the cabin intake path.

A second, more complex possibility involves the integration with the G35's engine management logic. Modern Infinity models often feature an AdBlue or DEF system managed by the Engine Control Unit (ECU). If the ECU detects a discrepancyâsuch as a missing pipe sensor, a lean air-fuel ratio reading due to the new pipe altering oxygen sensor readings, or a pressure fault in the DEF tankâit may enter a "limp mode." In this state, the ECU might disable urea injection entirely to prevent engine damage from unburned fuel accumulation. Without urea injection, there is no ammonia generation intended for reduction, but if there is residual fluid or if the system logic is confused regarding the new hardware configuration, you might detect smells associated with raw fuel combustion byproducts that mimic chemical odors, though true ammonia usually points to active but inefficient SCR chemistry.

Another potential pitfall in aftermarket exhaust work is the location of the connection points relative to the catalytic converters. If the new pipe connects downstream of the primary catalyst but upstream of the secondary reduction stage, or if it disrupts the thermal gradient required for the SCR process, the chemistry fails. The reaction between ammonia and $NO_x$ requires specific temperatures, typically exceeding 200Â°C. If the new pipe introduces excessive cooling via inadequate insulation or improper routing through shaded areas, the temperature drop can halt the catalytic reaction mid-process, allowing ammonia to escape unreacted.

To troubleshoot this without disassembling the vehicle immediately, check the DEF tank level and quality first. Contaminated urea with nitrites or nitrates will render the system ineffective, leading to immediate smell issues regardless of hardware changes. Next, inspect the new exhaust pipe for any visible leaks around flanges or welds where unburned gases might escape before entering the catalytic chamber. Finally, monitor the dashboard for any Service Engine Soon lights or specific emission fault codes (P-codes), as the ECU will often log a "Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold" code when ammonia slip is detected.

If the hardware installation appears sound and fluid quality is confirmed, the issue may lie in the catalyst bed itself. Sometimes, swapping an exhaust pipe inadvertently removes or damages the integrated catalytic substrate that was originally mounted within the system. Without the proper catalyst surface area, the ammonia cannot be converted back into nitrogen gas efficiently. In such cases, replacing the entire SCR-ready exhaust assembly or adding a dedicated catalytic converter designed for urea reduction is necessary to restore compliance and eliminate the odor.
